text_fidelity_a:
SABRENT Rocket Q 500GB NVMe PCIe M.2 2280 Internal SSD High Performance Solid State Drive R/W 2000/1000MB/s (SB-RKTQ-500) Compared to the Crucial 1TB M2 NVME I reviewed earlier, this Sabrent 512GB model benchmarks a little faster. And it works just fine on a PCI M2 adapter card, which are only a few bucks. (I bought the cheapest one available and it works.)

The NVME still offers much faster R/W speeds than other drives even when used with SATA 1 (as on my workstation). For example, the SSD I was using as my hard disk benchmarks at about 220MB/second. The Sabrent NVME on a PCI card benchmarks at about 1.5GB/second.

This time I experimented to see if I could get Debian Linux distro running on the NVME on my older workstation.

It took a few tries. Getting the OS to boot directly from the NVME was a no-go. Since the NVME is mounted on an adapter card, I had hoped it would trick the system into thinking it was just an ordinary SATA drive and boot from it. But that didn't happen.

So what I did was installed all the Linux OS EXCEPT for the boot folder on the NVME, and put the boot folder on the SSD HDD. So it boots from the SSD but the entire OS is on the NVME and runs from it.

Step one:

The partition manager in the Debian installer didn't want to partition the NVME at first.

So I bailed out of it and used GParted (Gnome disks utility couldn't do this) to "create partition table" and selected msdos as type. That wiped everything and turned the whole drive into unallocated space. From that point the partition manager worked.

Step two:

From the linux bootable USB installer I partitioned the SSD (not the NVME) with a primary partition labeled (to be mounted) as /boot. (You can make this partition most any size from a few GB on up---the boot files don't require a lot of space.) The remaining space I manually labeled as /msc.

I partitioned the NVME so the installer would put everything else on it, starting with / (root). You can simply make the whole NVME / root and the installer will take care of putting everything else on that drive, or you can do what I did and set up size-defined partitions for /home, /usr, and so on.

After installing the system, the installer asks where you want the bootloader GRUB installed. I selected the SSD.

It worked. The SSD does the booting to the NVME, which then runs the OS. And it did improve speed.
text_fidelity_b: SABRENT Rocket Q 500GB NVMe PCIe M.2 2280 Internal SSD High Performance Solid State Drive R/W 2000/1000MB/s (SB-RKTQ-500)

text_fidelity_a:
Antennas Direct DB2 Multi Directional HDTV Antenna (Discontinued by Manufacturer) I recently purchase an Antenna's Direct Clearstream 4 to use in my attic to feed the TVs in the BR and LR. Works fantastic, so when I needed another antenna for a TV in the study that I could not hook up to the antenna in the attic, I again went with Antenna's Direct, but this time picked the DB2 since it was smaller (and cheaper).

Absolutely fantastic reception! The only station it does not pull in as well as the Clearstream 4 was one fringe station. As with the Clearstream 4 positioning is a breeze - I just propped it up in the corner!

Given how well it performs, I thought I'd see how it does in the attic in place of the much larger and more expensive Clearstream. It does nearly as well - all the major networks come in equally good, and the DB2 picks up all but one of the more distant stations. The one it misses is a channel I never watch anyway, so for me, the two are equal.

For me (located outside Wash DC) the antennas pull in 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 5, 7.1, 7.2, 7.3, 9.1, 9.2, 14.1, 20.1, and about a dozen PBS stations rock solid. Channels 66.1 to 66.4 are so-so on the DB2 and pretty good on the Clearstream 4.

The Clearstream 4 also pulls in several analog stations. I didn't try that with the DB2 so I don't know if it will work with analog. Come February, the point will be moot anyway, so I didn't bother to test it out for analog.

So, if you're debating between the Clearstream 4 and the DB2 (or DB4), give the DB2 a shot first - the little guy may do the trick, and you can save quite a bit of cash.
text_fidelity_b: Antennas Direct DB2 Multi Directional HDTV Antenna (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

Tiffen 82VND 82 Millimeter Variable ND Filter I have one of the 77mm versions of this variable neutral density for cutting sunlight to manageable levels when shooting video outdoors. It works fine. I assume this 58mm version will work with typical Tiffen quality as well.

For those of you who might want to use it in conjunction with your factory lens hood, forget it.

The attaching thread is 58mm in diameter, but the outer diameter is 70.1 mm -- way bigger than the sunshade.

The front ring is threaded, but apparently only so the retaining ring can hold the front polarizer in place. The front thread measures out to 66.34mm to the inside of the thread (top of thread), or about 66.5 mm to the bottom of the thread groove. 67mm lens hoods exist and may fit, but not sure.

For my 77mm filter, I found a spare rubber lens shade that happened to be the same outer diameter as the filter and attached it with some electrician's tape. Works fine for longer lenses like the 70-200mm but vignettes on the 24mm end of the 24-70mm.

May need a matte box.

Comes in a very well built ballistic nylon pouch with Velcro closure and a very handy vinyl business card-sized window so you can label the thing and know what's inside.

It's a great filter that lets you shoot at 1/50 of a second at ISO 200 with the lens opened up to wider apertures to achieve shallow depth of field in bright sunlight. I find myself adjusting exposure by turning the filter a bit instead of changing f/stop.

Highly recommended. Just remember that you may be fighting flare unless you can rig up a sunshade, French flag or a matte box to keep the sun off it.
text_fidelity_b: Tiffen 82VND 82 Millimeter Variable ND Filter

text_fidelity_a:
Zinwell ZAT-970A Digital to Analog TV Converter Box (for Antenna Use) We needed to save some money, and I'd heard that Over The Air broadcasts included channels you wouldn't otherwise get. My Dish TV account provided local channels and a whole bunch of channels I didn't use; but the OTA feature really helps!

I paired the Zinwell digital / analog converter box (highly rated, outstanding Amazon price) with the Radio Shack Antennacraft® HDX1000 Amplified HDTV Antenna (also highly rated). You should know one thing -- the mast size for the Dish TV is larger than the mast size for the Antennacraft antenna, so you can't just remove the Dish and replace it with the Antennacraft on the same mast. But it is an easy install.

As a trial, before going up to the roof (2 story house), I set the Antennacraft in the downstairs window that has a view to the southwest (the direction our local TV stations broadcast from). Without the Zinwell, you're limited to the low power analog stations (mostly Spanish language, a few home shopping stations). I think I got about 6 stations. Then I plugged in the Zinwell in line between the antenna and the TV (after disconnecting the Dish TV feed), did a scan, and had 20 channels. Repeated the process upstairs (remember, we have a 2 story) and had 22 channels!! All the local tv stations (NBC, ABC, CW, ION, PBS, etc.) that broadcast digitally came through great!! Unfortunately, it started raining :( so after the rain stopped, I only got as far as getting the mast installed outdoors before it got too dark. It won't take long to finish.

Only one Zinwell related item: You're supposed to be able to choose the feed from the Zinwell to the TV to be either Coax or the Composite (yellow video, red and white audio). I couldn't get the composite to work in setup, but the coax worked just fine. Haven't had a chance to see if, once programmed, the composite would work, or if for some reason I hooked it up to my tv incorrectly (hard to imagine), but ... since the coax works so well, and video and audio quality are great, I'm money ahead and not complaining!!

So when do I break even? $80 antenna plus 2 $40 boxes = $160; Dish TV was costing me about $55/month (yeah, once you've been a subscriber for a while, there's essentially no customer retention policy, so, good by Dish!! -- and that's probably true for Directv and Comcast, too). So after 3 months, essentially at the start of January, I'm home free!! Thanks, Amazon, you're helping me save money, and that's really great!!

NOTE: I only ordered one Zinwell to test out things, now I've ordered a second for our other TV (didn't want to put too much at risk if it didn't work, but it works great!).

NOTE 2: The gov't coupon program is long dead, no hope of getting $40 off on one, just be glad if you waited that these things are as reasonably priced as they are.
text_fidelity_b: Zinwell ZAT-970A Digital to Analog TV Converter Box (for Antenna Use)

text_fidelity_a:
Amazon Fire TV - 1st Generation This is a great streaming box! Like the title says, it's a ROKU on steroids. I have an Apple Airport Extreme router and the ROKU would "occasionally" start buffering because of the processor; however, with the Amazon Fire TV, that's not an issue because it has a quad-core processor. Great streaming box!

Updated 5-4-14 I've had the Fire TV for a couple of months now and for the most part it's great; however, today we rented "Bad Grandpa" on Amazon. It played great but when there was 35 mins left in the movie, it quit playing. Tried to restart the movie and got a message saying there was a problem with playing the movie and to contact Amazon Customer Service. I called them and they said that when this happens, "...unplug the Fire TV for 15 seconds and then plug it back in." In my opinion, that takes the fun out of watching a movie! I thought the memory and quad-core processor would be enough to stop this from happening, wrong! Having said that, instead of naming my review "ROKU on Steroids" I should have named it "Just like ROKU".

The Amazon rep said that it was a problem with the memory of the Amazon Fire TV and not the video. When asked if the problem could be fixed by Amazon with an update, all he said was "I'll forward that to Amazon".

If you don't mind watching videos that stop playing and having to unplug the Fire TV and restart it during a movie, you'll really like the Fire TV.

One other point, the Amazon rep stated that it might be my router. I have an Apple Airport Extreme, the best and fastest available. If it was my router, I guess the Amazon rep should have had me unplug my router instead of the Fire TV. He finally admitted that it was the Fire TV and not the router.

Just wanted to get this information out there so people can be informed about the Amazon Fire TV before purchasing one. All in all, I'm happy with the Fire TV...just aggravated that I have to unplug it and restart it when watching movies. The Amazon Fire TV should be better than this!
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Fire TV - 1st Generation

text_fidelity_a:
ZyXEL 300 Mbps Wireless N Access Point, Ethernet Client, Universal Repeater, and Range Extender (WAP3205) Overall this is a good little feature-rich device but use just the wireless access point features. It was quick to setup but was definitely a time that you wanted to read the fine manual (RTFM (PG version)). It wasn't as easy to setup as the CISCO WES610N that I purchased at the same time BUT it is also feature rich.

I have had it up for a few days and haven't experienced major problems with it. We will see if it stands up to the test of time and gives me 3-4 years of service like my Cisco Linksys devices that are still working 4 1/2 years later.

Nerd Alert - I am a nerd at heart and utilize geek speak way too often. I try to remember that the Amazon audience contains friends, family, and strangers that may or may not know IT.

PROS:
* Feature Rich -
The ZyXEL is 1/2 the price of the comparable Cisco device but it has a much more feature rich set of wireless capabilities. It supports WPS, allowing for easy setup. It supports WDS, allowing you to configure a network that allows you to carry your laptop from room to room in a large house without sacrificing much speed if setup correctly. It can access as a repeater if needed.

* Cabling -
The ZyXEL includes the power supply and a network cable (CAT-5). It supports a standard called MDI/MDIX, which means that you won't need a crossover cable if you connect it to a switch.
* Wireless Distribution Service -
You can make this part of your existing network using WDS, or Wireless Distribution Service, or simply configure it as an access point. I just removed two old Linksys routers from being WDS nodes since replacing my old Actiontec 802.11a/b/g with an Actiontec 802.11b/g/n wireless router. Eventually I will get around to using the ONI port and setting up a network with DD-WRT

CONS:
* LAN ports on the back are are 10/100 -
While the router notes that it supports connection speeds up to 300MbPS it only has two (2) 10MbPS/100MbPS RJ-45 (LAN) connections. Technically you may never truly realize the full throughput available with this device. This is not unlike other wireless access points, such as the Cisco WET610N (single 10/100) or the Cisco WES610N (quad port 10/100 for $10 more). I did what any good geek would do; used it as an excuse to purchase an 8-port Netgear 10/100/1000 switch to replace my 5-port 10/100 switch in my office/lab with the computers and Hyper-V lab systems. I am going to use the Cisco product downstairs with my home server and VMWare ESXi box.

* Setup may be difficult for the average home user -
I most certainly RTFM'd and reading the manual helped. It did take a quick configuration of my network card in order to even get to the point I could setup the device.
The Cisco devices use an APIPA address, which makes setup easier. Why? APIPA is that 169.254.#.# address that your computer gets when it connects to a network that doesn't give out addresses. This allows you to easily setup the Cisco WES610N.
text_fidelity_b: ZyXEL 300 Mbps Wireless N Access Point, Ethernet Client, Universal Repeater, and Range Extender (WAP3205)

text_fidelity_a:
Creative Sound Blaster Roar 2 Portable NFC Bluetooth Speaker with aptX/AAC (Black) I’m a big fan of the Roar since it provides me with two key benefits: great sound and is easy to use. The Roar 2 retains those two benefits and adds one more: a smaller footprint. I’m going to try my best to not overuse the words “outstanding” and "impressive" in this review, but it’s going to be a challenge. This is an impressive speaker.

The out-of-the-box experience is nicely done. As expected at this price point, it comes in upscale packaging. More important, it comes with a pretty decent user guide. That’s significant since the Roar 2 has a lot of features – to call it just “a speaker” really shortchanges it. It’s also a recorder, a power bank, an MP3 player, an SD card reader, a speakerphone – it will even lull you to sleep with Bedtime Mode where it gradually decreases the volume and then powers off. My only complaint about the manual is that it’s physically small, which means the type size is also small. I do wish manufacturers would realize that those of us with aging eyes still like loud music!

And loud music is this product’s forte. I’m able to get room-filling sound while maintaining crisp highs, clear midrange and solid but not muddy bass. I can even go past room-filling to the “let’s annoy the neighbors” levels and still maintain impressive fidelity. Using the Tera Bass option boosts the bass response to the point where you would swear there was a separate subwoofer on the floor. You can see the end plates resonate to help drive the bass (plus it just looks really cool as well).

Day to day usage of the Roar 2 is straightforward even though there are so many features. All the buttons are labeled fairly clearly, albeit at times with small type. I would also have preferred a greater contrast to the labels since sometimes they are hard to see unless the Roar 2 is under a bright light. There are voice prompts for many key features which I found helpful. Normally I don’t care for voice prompts, but these were done in a natural sounding voice at a low volume making them not at all irritating. But, if you don’t like them at all, you can turn them off. There are small, but clear indicator lights to keep you apprised of battery charge level, settings, and other criteria.

The build quality is excellent. This feels as good as it looks, with a solid heft to it, an excellent quality metal grill, and quality plastic case components. All the buttons have a good tactile feel to them. I have it in white, which looks very nice with the gray contrast control pad. My only quibble is that some of the buttons/levers are on the small side. However, those tend to be the lesser used function. The main function buttons (on/off, volume, pairing, Tera Bass, etc.) are larger and easy to use.

The Roar 2 is not inexpensive, but the performance, build quality and features make it an excellent value. If you enjoy great sound and need to keep to a small footprint speaker, these should absolutely be on your short list (and at the top of it by a wide margin). Highly, highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Creative Sound Blaster Roar 2 Portable NFC Bluetooth Speaker with aptX/AAC (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
SanDisk Ultra Fit 128GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive - SDCZ43-128G-GAM46 I've always been really happy with SanDisk cards and flash drives, both for speed and reliability, unhesitatingly recommending them vs playing data roulette with generic drives. So I didn't really think twice when I needed to upgrade to a 128GB flashdrive from my smaller ones, I just ordered another SanDisk Ultra Fit.
Oops. No more.
The many other reviews are correct. This drive has serious overheating problems.
It works great if you're not trying to write more than a few GB at a time.
It also works pretty well in an external USB Hub, wrapped in ice packs. But that's not exactly practical, and completely defeats the purpose of getting a small form factor drive in the first place.
It also works okay if I intentionally throttle data transfer 30%-50%, but that's really pretty pointless, isn't it?
So it's not bad for storing data, photos, video, etc., as long as you don't mind setting up ice packs for the initial loading. But useless for backups, hosting virtual machines, sneaker net, or any other data intensive operation.
Basically useless for at least half of what I wanted it for.
And SanDisk's generic response "SanDisk drives comply with industry specific standards and are tested to remain in acceptable temperature ranges under normal operating conditions" is pretty darn useless too.
[Edit] Be aware that when it overheats it starts randomly disconnecting. This will corrupt datafiles being written ***without any warning***. If you care about your data, you need to do a CRC or full binary compare after copying data to this drive.
text_fidelity_b: SanDisk Ultra Fit 128GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive - SDCZ43-128G-GAM46

text_fidelity_a:
ContourROAM Hands-free HD Camcorder Picked up a couple of these when Amazon had them on sale for half price. Had to return one because it was out of focus; Amazon processed the return quickly and the replacement works great.

Very pleased with the image quality of these cameras in the 1080p mode (which I always use). The video quality is sharp and colorful. Make sure you use the camera software to set the image quality to the highest level for best results.

Sound quality is a mixed bag. This camera uses noise reduction to reduce wind noise (which is a big problem with older Contour cameras at even moderate bicycling speeds), but the noise reduction also severely muffles your voice if you are trying to narrate a video while filming.

The camera controls are very easy to use, which is an improvement over earlier Contour cameras. The instant-on feature works great if you're filming only pieces of your event. I get about 3 hours of video from one battery charge. That also seems to be the amount of video that fits on a 32GB microSD card. If your event is longer than 3 hours, use the instant-on/instant-off feature to switch the camera on for just the important parts. The instant-on feature is a nice improvement over earlier Contour cameras that are difficult to turn on when you are moving.

Contour cameras seem to go on sale more often than GoPro. If you can catch it at a good sale price, I think Contour is a much better value than GoPro.
text_fidelity_b: ContourROAM Hands-free HD Camcorder

text_fidelity_a:
ARRIS SURFboard SB6141 8x4 DOCSIS 3.0 Cable Modem - Retail Packaging- White Update Jan 2016: After only a few months of use, the modem started acting up. At first, a reboot would cure the problem, but it got progressively worse whereas I needed to reboot it every few hours. It then failed to work at all even though all the indicator lights were indicating it was functioning properly. Swapped it with a different modem and all the problems went away.

Normally I would not down rate an item because of a failure since everything can break. However, if you expect to get warranty support for this, forget it. Arris/Motorola will not stand behind their product at all.

If you're OK with this being disposable when it breaks, go for it. It did work well when it was working. But, if you expect to get warranty support/repair/replacement, go for another brand.

Original review:
So far this has been a champ in terms of performance. I'm using it with Cox, and it replaces another DOCSIS 3.0 modem I had been using for the past four years (a Motorola SB6120). I got it mainly because I was concerned that my old modem would eventually die on me, and wanted to have a backup.

Installation was simple (just a quick call to Cox to give them the MAC id and serial number). Connection speeds have been slightly better than the SB6120 and more consistent. This seems to run no warmer than the SB6120, which is to say it's pretty warm but not hot when operating. The indicator lights are brighter on this model which, for me, is not a problem given where I have the modem located, but could be an issue if you have your modem out in the open -- the lights are beacon-bright in a dark room.

I'm hoping to get the same solid, dependable performance out of this that my SB6120 gave me. I'll update the review should reliability prove to be a problem down the road. But, at present, this is performing perfectly.
text_fidelity_b: ARRIS SURFboard SB6141 8x4 DOCSIS 3.0 Cable Modem - Retail Packaging- White

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech G240 Cloth Gaming Mouse Pad for Low-DPI Gaming I'm not a gamer. I wanted to try this mouse pad out for graphics (photo editing, vector graphics, and so forth). I'm not a big fan of pen-type tablet input devices. I've always preferred working with a mouse. (To me, the only real down side to using a mouse instead of a tablet input is loss of pressure sensitivity, but there are plenty of workarounds.)

This pad works great. An optical/laser mouse reads it very well, with the slightest movements picked up. The bottom of the pad is grippy enough for the pad to stay put, and the surface, while satin-like, still has enough resistance to provide a lot of fine control.

It's also larger than I expected. It's 11 inches by 13.5 inches. And it is quite flexible and rolls up easily for storage or transport.

Here are some tips for getting precise mouse control:

First of all understand that a low-DPI setting means your pointer doesn't move far when you move the mouse. This enables gamers to aim and target precisely in-game. It also enables artists to precisely move the pointers when working on graphics. How far your cursor/pointer moves is entirely up to you and can be adjusted in your control panel for pointer settings (or, depending on the game, possibly can be adjusted in your game settings).

In that control panel, uncheck "enhance pointer precision." This will turn off pointer acceleration, which can adversely affect control. If the software (or game) you're using overrides this (rare in graphics software, but more common in games), you may have to employ a fix. Just do a search for "Windows 7/8 mouse fix" and you'll find plenty of information on how to do this.

Anyway, it's a great pad for precision cursor control with a mouse, whether for gaming or graphics.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech G240 Cloth Gaming Mouse Pad for Low-DPI Gaming

The problem is, in order to use this amplifier with my phone, I have only two choices: (1) Sit still, since it is not possible to freely move around with my phone while listening to music using headphones and this amplifier as I can do when I use Bluetooth earbuds, since this device does not have Bluetooth transmitter capability. text_fidelity_a:
JVC Soft Wireless Earbud with Stayfit Tips, Remote and Mic and Bluetooth Violet (HA-FX9BTV) 3.5 stars taking price into account

With headphones, it is always a blend of "you get what you paid for", and comparing to others at a similar price point.
How do these compare? Well, they are about average for the $20-$40 range. Not much better, not much worse. And as is the case with headphones, for a bit more, you can do MUCH better, and for a bit less, you will get roughly similar results. (In other words, headphones under $75-$100 are, more or less very similar, and then suddenly, your options get drastically better.)

Here's my analysis on the general sound quality and other features:

MISC:
Phone calls: 5 stars: Easy to use, works great for calls on both ends, and blocks outside sound quite well!
Ease of use/pairing: 5 stars: It passed the test of not having to read instructions, meaning it is incredibly simple to pair and use
Appearance: 5 stars: Neat! It's colorful and fun, as well as practical and functional!
External noise: 4 stars: Because it has a pretty tight seal, it is like an earplug, blocking outside sound quite effectively
Comfort: 3 stars: comparable to others of this design. Totally fine at first, and annoying after long use.

SOUND:
Treble: 2 stars: quite tinny
Bass: 2 stars: ok depth, not great, not very powerful
Overall: 2 stars: not much detail in the sound, but it can get pretty loud without distorting, and it is definitely good enough for basic listening and phone calls. There also appears to be a *very slight* hiss in quiet/silent moments when the volume is louder.

OVERALL:
The average is 28 out of 40 possible points, or 70% (a "C" grade, if it were going to school ;-), but because the above analysis does not take price point into account, comparing this to brands like Bose, as well as dollar store headphones, this means that for the current list price of roughly $29.99, this is a reasonable expectation.

The average number of stars based on my rubric is 3.5 stars: decent for this price point, and certainly good enough to enjoy music and spoken word, and to have successful phone calls.
text_fidelity_b: JVC Soft Wireless Earbud with Stayfit Tips, Remote and Mic and Bluetooth Violet (HA-FX9BTV)

WD My Net AC1300 HD Dual Band Router Wireless AC WiFi Router Accelerate HD UPDATE: Since the review below this paragraph, I have put this up without a backup, and it's been a fire and forget mission. No problems with wireless network service. My "OK" review still stands, but I'm still optimistic some firmware upgrades or a big "that's it!" on my end could get everything working better or even flawlessly.

I have an extensive wired gigabit network in my home, so it has not been my top priority to replace my antiquated wireless B/G router (although I do use it much for casual surfing, mind you). Because I've been very busy when at home lately and in no mood to deal with nuisance computer/network issues, I put this new router in parallel with the old so that if issues came up, I wouldn't have to deal with them immediately. After about three weeks, albeit with only casual and sporadic "trying to make it work right", it's still not ready to run solo, obviously reason enough to just rate average.

This is unfortunate because it has a lot of cool touted features. The funny thing is when I was first setting it up I was thinking how they really have it idiot-proofed - even the WAN port is color coded to the included network cable (they don't even call it a WAN port, BTW).

But as is so often the case, by trying to make something useable to the masses, it actually becomes more difficult for advanced users to do simple tasks: I sort of want some Network Attached Storage (NAS), but have been too cheap/lazy/power misery to want to bother dealing with it, so I thought it would be great to try this router with its USB ports - ideally, I was going to put some hard drives in my gun safe, which is beside my telecom closet, and attach them to the router via USB, and have them both set to turn off when not in use. But it's just not working. I could go into a rant here about how Windows tries to set up a GUI so that people ignorant to computers can access their media when I all I really want to do is access the root of the drives and then do what I want without interference, but I'll save you my usual rant because I don't want you to misinterpret that it is indeed the router's fault that it rarely recognizes my attached devices (although interaction with various versions of Windows is the fault of both companies). The fact is, from the router's access page, you can see that my drives are often not recognized at all, or the router still thinks I have something attached that I've detached a while back (and sometimes even after a reboot). Clearly, I'm not about to put these drives down in a safe on another floor; it's easier just to deal with them locally. I was unable to EVER access these from a tablet or a phone; I wasn't about to waste that much time when I couldn't even rely on it to work with decent Windows machines.

The gigabit Ethernet ports are a great feature, and the wireless portion works better, but there have been a few times where I've checked my machines and they've reverted back to my legacy network, meaning that the new router obviously went down, if only for a short time. Thus, I'm not ready to put this machine up solo and deal with any headaches that I may have to incur.

With some cool features like QoS (Quality of Service) and port forwarding, etc., it sounds like it could be a great router. I can't begin to test these well when I'm still frustrated with making it look like a real seamless network. These are probably things that can and will be fixed with firmware updates, but they should have had this ironed out before release. If I hear of a good update, I'll give it another go if I'm still interested and will let you know how it works out.
text_fidelity_b: WD My Net AC1300 HD Dual Band Router Wireless AC WiFi Router Accelerate HD

text_fidelity_a:
SanDisk SDSSDX-120G-G25 Extreme SSD 120GB SATA 6.0 Gb-s2.5-Inch Solid State Drive (SSD) A great product that works as described.

After flashing the SSD firmware from a bootable CD, putting a 120gb SanDisk Extreme in a (Dell GX620 sff/3ghz Pentium Dual Core w/2gb of RAM) was a walk in the park and so was installing Linux Mint 13 Cinnamon on the SSD. Enabling the Trim function as described on various Mint/Ubuntu websites went without a hitch. I've enabled a few other basic tweaks and they also have worked without any problems. Be sure to use the the EXT4 file system when partitioning, Linux Mint 13 uses it by default. Do not use the Linux Mint 13 KDE release, not even Orkin could kill all the bugs on that turkey.

At this point I am using the swap partition and browser caching on the SSD, but will be moving those to RAM as soon as Amazon gets my memory delivered to bump my computer up to 4gb. A note to other Dell GX620 owners. The Normal mode in the BIOS is in fact AHCI mode, as such it does fully support the Trim function. Linux can also emulate the Trim function using CRON if you do not have an AHCI capable box.

I'm telling you all this because getting the information to determine whether an SSD would work on my computer was like pulling teeth. User Name "SpeedStep" on the Dell forums was a lot of help.

Buy an SSD, you'll like it. Unless your Mac or an XP user, it isn't that big a deal.
text_fidelity_b: SanDisk SDSSDX-120G-G25 Extreme SSD 120GB SATA 6.0 Gb-s2.5-Inch Solid State Drive (SSD)

text_fidelity_a:
Masione 4 Pack Outdoor Fake/Dummy Security Camera with 30 Illuminating LED Light (Silver) CCTV Surveillance [[VIDEOID:ecbfab27d25a92fd322c831d655b23cd]] UPDATED REVIEW 09/25/17:
... apparently they looked SO realistic someone stole the camera itself, lol. I bet they were surprised when they got it home. These still did the trick for awhile at least. I have yet to replace the stolen one, but they are a good deterrent.

ORIGINAL REVIEW
of discounted product

I have had these a couple of months now. I purchased these because we had some mail stolen out of our mailbox. We live on a larger parcel of property and the main gate is a ways from the main house. We are building a package drop box, but until then I needed something more immediate.

I realize someone, upon close inspection will know these are fake, but sometimes a good deterrent is all one needs. I attached these near a power source so it would at least kind of look real. I also put a fake antennae of my own nearby so it would look like it was transmitting wirelessly. I put some electrical tape here and there to make it look like wires running. It was a quick attempt, but for me, it will at least make someone think twice. I will eventually put a game camera out there, more hidden, so then the dummy camera will take the attention off the real camera.

So $5/each for these hulls is not a bad retail price. You add (4) AA batteries and it lights it up at night with an 'infrared" so it looks more real. The infrared is motion sensitive and seems to work well. The top cover slides on to protect the batteries and that too seems to work well.

These were exactly what I was looking for. I searched these out specifically. Until we can afford real cameras that work wirelessly, that far from our house, these deterrents will have to do.

I find no cons with these during the several weeks I have had them in my possession. No regrets.
text_fidelity_b: Masione 4 Pack Outdoor Fake/Dummy Security Camera with 30 Illuminating LED Light (Silver) CCTV Surveillance

Philips BT2500B/37 Wireless Portable Speaker The portability is excellent, as well as a few other features: it is rechargeable, very small, lightweight, and the pairing process is so easy. Unfortunately, this product has several downsides, and they are the ones that count most: the sound quality is bad.

I always wonder why products allow you to raise the volume far beyond the limits of what the product can sustain without creating distortion. The point at which the product does this is roughly halfway; it can only go to roughly 65-80 decibels before treble starts to sound horrible, distorted, and messy. That is NOT very loud at all. The sound, even at lower volumes, is somewhat fuzzy: you cannot hear detail in the music like you can with better quality speakers. Even With the distortion, at maximum volume, it doesn't get Very loud. That's mostly to be expected at this price point and in something of this size with rechargeable batteries, you can't hope for much more than this product has to offer. For that reason, it gets 3 stars. Roughly average--not great, not terrible.
text_fidelity_b: Philips BT2500B/37 Wireless Portable Speaker

Motorola MB8600 DOCSIS 3.1 Cable Modem - Approved for Comcast Xfinity, Cox, and Charter Spectrum, Supports Cable Plans up to 1000 Mbps | 1 Gbps Ethernet Port I recently purchased this to replace a 1gb modem that I was struggling with periodically. I thought a support version for Comcast may help. I was wrong...the new modem exacerbated the situation where I was having drops more frequently and longer. After plenty of research and validating through forums that I may have a bad line/connection. (TBC) The reason I say this is because I am seeing these errors in the modem logs: No Ranging Response received - T3 time-out;

I am pretty confident the people complaining about drops on the 1 star are going through the same thing.. The old modems may not have been as sensitive...

Steps I am taking to confirm/resolve:
1. Comcast is coming tomorrow to test form CO to house.
2. If no issue there, I am going to ask for a new cable to be run from CO to where my modem is (no break in line that degrades signal) I am not going to hold my breath on this as all my stats are within tolerance range including Freq. (MHz), Pwr (dBmV), SNR (dB)...
3. Opened ticket with Motorola to see a) if they will respond b) if any new firmware or actions they recommend such as tweaking somehow.
4. If all else fails, send this back and try another..

Keep you posted..
3. Dump this modem and try another one

Update 11/21 - Very briefly:
1. Comcast technician said cable issue (as I suspected)
2. Motorola support is quite responsive. However, they said defective modem
3. I replaced the cable and started RMA

It was the cable. I have had 1 error in 48 hours. I was getting errors every 2 hours prior to.

1/27/22 - The drops every 2-6 hours are back. Worked with Xfinity and confirmed all inbound was fine. Replaced with old CM1000 which had zero failures. This modem is finally going back. Reliability is questions.
text_fidelity_b: Motorola MB8600 DOCSIS 3.1 Cable Modem - Approved for Comcast Xfinity, Cox, and Charter Spectrum, Supports Cable Plans up to 1000 Mbps | 1 Gbps Ethernet Port

text_fidelity_a:
Orion 8923 20mm Expanse Telescope Eyepiece I have an Orion SkyQuest XT6 for over 10 years, and I've only had 3 eyepieces the whole time. Their standard Sirius Plossl 25mm, 17mm and 10mm. For the most part, the 10mm is pretty much useless, as the field of vision is so narrow that constant adjustments need to be made. I decided to give the Expanse series a try. This eyepiece is by far the best in the of the 4. Near Detroit, the light pollution is pretty bad. Viewing the plants and the moon is usually OK. My previous higher powered eyepieces usually made things look really bright and blurry. The Orion Nebula is usually a grey smudge. With the 9mm Expanse, I was able to see more shape to the cloud, and even a handful of stars in its heart. Cloud bands on Jupiter never looked better! I was also able to get a significant amount more detail on the moons surface than what I am used to. Looking at the sun was uneventful today -- only two sunspots.

Ultimately, this is definitely worth buying!
text_fidelity_b: Orion 8923 20mm Expanse Telescope Eyepiece

ProtoArc Wireless Bluetooth Trackball Mouse, EM01 2.4G RGB Ergonomic Rechargeable Rollerball Mice, 3 Device Connection&Thumb Control, Compatible for PC, iPad, Mac, Windows-White Silver I switch between a Logitech M570 (thumb trackball) and a Logitech MX Master 3 (regular mouse) daily, so I couldn’t help but compare the ProtoArc Trackball to the devices I use daily. For me, it’s not a worthy replacement. It’s a backup mouse, or one to take traveling with me when I’m worried my favorite mice might get damaged or lost.

I do really like the adjustable angle of the mouse itself. The base allows you to set the mouse at 0 degrees or 20 degrees. That feature drew me to the trackball, and I think it’s implemented well. The mouse is rock steady at 0 or 20 degrees, but it’s easy to switch between the options. And because it’s built in, there are no extra parts to carry or worry about losing. For me, the 20 degree angle feels very natural, and that’s the one thing I miss when I go back to my usual mice.

The trackball itself feels sluggish and inconsistent. I’ve tried adjusting the DPI, but that’s not the problem. Sometimes the ball registers the movement of my thumb and sometimes it doesn’t. I did check the ball and sensors; they are clean. The ball is actually hard to pop out, I needed to stick a pen through the small hole to get it out.

The left and right click are soft and muted sounding. Which is okay, but then the scroll wheel click is loud in comparison. The scroll wheel has some resistance, it’s like scrolling through quicksand.

The mouse charges via USB-C.
text_fidelity_b: ProtoArc Wireless Bluetooth Trackball Mouse, EM01 2.4G RGB Ergonomic Rechargeable Rollerball Mice, 3 Device Connection&Thumb Control, Compatible for PC, iPad, Mac, Windows-White Silver

text_fidelity_a:
Microsoft Surface Book 13.5" (Intel Core i5, 8GB RAM, 256 GB) We have a number of surface tablets in our house, and this was my first surface book. I got it hoping for some increased performance for using with my landscape CAD program, and I did notice a difference in the smoothness when working with CAD on this device as opposed to my other comparable surface tablets. The better performance only works when it is hooked up to the keyboard, which is fine for CAD work.

I also like to use this as a tablet for photo editing work related to my business, and here I noticed my number one complaint about this device, which is that the tablet part itself does not have the little foldout stand that all of the other surface tablets have. I guess they think that you will just connect it to the keyboard, but sometimes I want it to be as flexible and lightweight as a regular surface Pro tablet, and while you can unhook it from the keyboard and use it as a tablet, it feels more bulky and the lack of stand makes it less flexible in its use than the surface Pro tablets.

One thing I did notice is that you can connect it to the keyboard backwards and use the keyboard as a stand that way, however that does not bend to the same angle as the tablet stands do on a regular surface Pro.

I also think that the battery life is a lot less on this one than on the surface Pro tablets. Even when not connected to the keyboard and the increased computing performance that you get from that, it seems to wear down its batteries on tablet mode in about 30 to 45 minutes of photo editing. When I worked on my surface tablet in this fashion, I feel like I got a little less than two hours before having to recharge.

Overall, if you plan to use this primarily plugged in as a laptop and only occasionally as a tablet, the increased performance from the attached keyboard make this a worthwhile choice if you do gaming or more high-powered computing. However, if you are primarily using it as a tablet or in places where battery life is a critical consideration, I would suggest the regular surface Pro tablet instead.

In terms of accessories, I use the surface pen constantly, but haven't reached for the other accessories much at all. The surface pen makes it so smooth to make notes on photographs to convey ideas to people, and is great for photo editing.
text_fidelity_b: Microsoft Surface Book 13.5" (Intel Core i5, 8GB RAM, 256 GB)

text_fidelity_a:
MOSISO Fashion Laptop Backpack for Women, Pure Deep Gray I am in love with this bag!
It has so many features that are important to me.
I plan on using this bag for day trips with the family and especially during my childrens' swim meets.
This bag has more compartments and zippers then I expected it to have.
There are three main large compartments, two small compartments in the front and an anti-theft pocket in the back and the side water bottle mesh are also contained in a pocket. I was a little worried that I wouldn't be able to fit my water bottle in the outside mesh since there is a zipper and extra fabric and stuff, but as you can see from my image, a sports drink bottle fits perfectly in there.
The bag comes with its own lock which can be programmed to your own code.
The bag has two padded sections within the two largest zippered areas. One for a laptop with a velcro strip and one in the middle section with no velcro.
I plan to use the middle padded area for my mp3 player as this is the area that the headphone cables enter into and I will also put my power bank in that padded area since this is also where the charger port comes from.
The color of this bag is very modern, it's a good bag for a male or female.
I like that I can zip shut the drink compartments if I wanted to have something in them that I don't want to fall out (skittles/sunflower seeds)!
There is a padded carry handle and a non-padded hanging handle which is really nice. The back is very padded as are the shoulder straps.
There is even a luggage strap for if I wanted to bring this on the plane trip.
There are two cinch straps above each water bottle which is nice, as sometimes I like to cinch in my jacket or if I had a lot of bulky stuff inside that could be cinched to remove air and the bulk.
The bag has the interior organization in the front large compartment, including a clip for your keys, two wider sections, mesh on one and two pencil holes, which is great for me as I like to bring a pencil, sharpie, and highlighter with me to the swim meets.
I like that there are so many large compartments, allowing me to keep my stuff separate. I like to bring magazines to read between heats and sometimes my laptop (rear), snacks in the middle and the schedule and journal in the front.
I like the smaller compartment to contain the emergency kit (bandaids, pain reliever, etc).
I don't think there is anything else in a bag that this bag doesn't have.
A great mom bag!
text_fidelity_b: MOSISO Fashion Laptop Backpack for Women, Pure Deep Gray

text_fidelity_a: Seagate Barracuda 7200 1 TB 7200RPM SATA 3Gb/s 32MB Cache 3.5 Inch Internal Hard Drive I'd give it negative 5 if I could. I was working on my computer one night. It froze.  I walked the dog.... came back. Still frozen. Reboot. No Operating system. Seatools said bad LBAs.  Then that died. Couldn't even get bad LBAs.  So I take the circuit board off and send it to be replaced with a new board, my chip. Put it in the computer. Computer sees it the CCxx version and all, but freezes and won't boot.  Walked the dog, came back, still nothing. So I buy a kit that communicates through the serial connection of the drive. Nothing. Won't read, won't write. How do I know. I thought I had backed up my drive but when I looked at the files saved on my back up drive, it had not saved anything for a year.  I had been noticing it freezes when I am trying to copy to a back up drive.  The thing that drives me crazy is it comes on and seems to work but won't do anything.  When I tried to format it, the computer shows the drive size in the format window, but says it can't format it. When I put it in a USB drive, windows recognized it was there but thinks it is 0 bytes.  I would never have bought a seagate in the first place but it came in a computer I purchased already built.  I used to make my own but thought it was cheaper to just buy. I got cheaper alright.
text_fidelity_b: Seagate Barracuda 7200 1 TB 7200RPM SATA 3Gb/s 32MB Cache 3.5 Inch Internal Hard Drive

Reading the reviews I decided on the TCL 55r615. The voice remote on the r617 wasn’t worth the extra fifty bucks, and the voice function is duplicated on the Roku phone app anyway.

I am VERY happy with the TV; Colors and picture are bright and contrast seems excellent. I’ve watched a couple of 4k documentaries and was blown away with the picture. The Roku menu for the streaming channels really is excellent to use: Far “Snappier” and easier to navigate than any other that I’ve used. (Including my Sony Blu-ray player) The Roku set up allows setting up the apps on your PC and updating the TV afterwards making initial set up a breeze. The Roku app allows listening with headphones to whatever is on the TV, but I haven’t used that yet. (I read where people have purchased older Roku remotes that have the headphone jack, but don’t need that function myself)

Since I read that many people had problems with Banding, I downloaded some test JPG’s to a thumb drive and tested the set: It passed! No banding was seen and colors were even with the exception of very slight darkening in the four corners. Even knowing it’s there, I can’t see it on live TV so I’m happy.

The bad parts: the screen is more reflective than my old set. Since I was going to wall mount the set anyways, I’ll point the screen downwards to minimize the glare. I’m certain the high end TVs costing 4 times as much have this covered, but I’m good with my TCL. Setting up my Directv remote to the set was a HUGE PITA. This was more a problem with the remote than the TCL set, but was an hour of my life I want back.

I haven’t tried using a sound bar with the ARC/CEC function, but I don’t anticipate any issues. Overall, I’m pleased to have found such high quality at this price-point and would recommend this set.

text_fidelity_a:
Acer Aspire R 15 2-in-1 Laptop, 15.6" Full HD Touch, 7th Gen Intel Core i7, GeForce 940MX, 12GB DDR4, 256GB SSD, R5-571TG-7229 This will be a fairly detailed and honest review.

1. Who is this for?
This computer is what I would consider a gateway computer. Those who are looking at upgrading a fairly old or not so powerful laptop and are looking to do a little more productivity, this is a great option.

2. What do you get?
Well you can probably read the description, however it's worth noting. You get an Intel i7 7500u CPU (dual core with 4 threads) 12gb DDR4 RAM, Nvidia 940mx GPU, a 256gb SSD, 15.6" 1080p screen, fingerprint reader, and a backlit keyboard.

The reason I mention all of the feautures is because you would be hardpressed to find another laptop with these features for the same price. To my knowledge there is not laptop on the market for $800 with an i7, dedicated graphics, 12gb of RAM and an SSD. This is really one of the best values on the market right now.

With all of that said, this isn't for everyone. If you want to do extensive gaming, this is not for you. Can it game? Yes, light gaming can be achieved, however it isn't marketed as a gaming laptop. Is this for someone who wants to do editing (video, audio, photos)? Yes, again light editing can be achieved.

What blew me away with this computer is the speakers! They are fantastic! I usually use headphones and would consider myself somewhat picky with sound, and for laptop speakers these are really something great.

This computer is really a middle of the pack all arounders dream. If you dabble in a little of this and a little of that but don't do anything professionally or extremely serious, this is really all you need.

Also, everyone's experience is different. Some hate loud fans, and if this is pushed the fans will be audible. Some don't like that the backlit keyboard times out after 30 seconds of no use. These things really don't bother me.

Lastly, the versatility of this laptop is really great. I've bought tablets and sold them because I couldn't justify having a laptop and tablet, then bought tablets again because I missed the things I could do with them that I was missing on a laptop. This solved all of those issues except size. It's pretty big, which for some is a plus others its not.

Overall, if you are looking at upgrading and don't want to spend $1,200-2,000 on a flagship model laptop this is a great option! I can't recommend this enough.
text_fidelity_b: Acer Aspire R 15 2-in-1 Laptop, 15.6" Full HD Touch, 7th Gen Intel Core i7, GeForce 940MX, 12GB DDR4, 256GB SSD, R5-571TG-7229

Fujifilm FinePix J40 12.2 MP Digital Camera with 3x Optical Zoom and 3-Inch LCD (Includes 2 GB SD Memory Card) The camera is $[..]for gosh sakes! It's an amazing little piece of technology. The 3X optics and 12.2MP CMOS camera are well matched in the optical train to provide a great image for casual photos adequate for most users. It's the simplest start-up I've ever seen. The viewer LCD provides a maximum size to the package. `The manual' is 7 steps of which 4 include inserting memory, battery, charging battery and turning it on. It's `point and shoot' in the extreme.

I work in the domain of optics & imaging design. My wife has a 5 year old Fuji camera of this same genre that I've gone to some lengths to compare with Nikon and Canon in this low cost market. Without getting technical ... for the old Fuji, there are no user discernable image quality differences. The Fuji optics were superior (i.e. best objective lens light capture and transfer). Take your pick between the 3 on the backend image processing system/PC interface.

My wife has carried the 5 year old Fuji in her purse every day ... that's a technically demanding reliability challenge. Fuji can be relied on to deliver the best value for money in an image capture platform if you're designing a million dollar platform or this $69 platform. You're not paying the premium for the huge advertisement budget of Nikon and Canon when you buy Fuji. I think you just get a better camera.

I can't speak to this unit's reliability for now. A 3x optical train with autofocus, f-stop, etc mechanisms and micro motors are robust to a point. They will all fail, even the highest dollar product, if exposed to the wrong environment (g-shock, sand, salt spray, thermal shock, etc).

One reviewer mentioned software loading problems. I had absolutely no problems on a Windows 7, 64bit OS.

You can't go wrong with this device. It's an excellent camera for you or the kids or the g-kids for Xmas.
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm FinePix J40 12.2 MP Digital Camera with 3x Optical Zoom and 3-Inch LCD (Includes 2 GB SD Memory Card)

text_fidelity_a:
Blink XT2 Outdoor/Indoor Smart Security Camera with cloud storage included, 2-way audio, 2-year battery life – 2 camera kit This was a real disappointment. One of the main problems is that it is only compatible with 2G and if you have a 2G and a 5G network it still may not work if your network is merged and/or you have intermittent 2G. Not sure if this applies to you? It probably does if you live in the United States in a major city. Secondly the support was terrible. Have you ever call a support line and it took 20 minutes just for them to get your name your email and whatever other information they claimed they need to identify its you? Well that's exactly the type of support you can expect from Blink. They take forever and I'm not exaggerating, forever to even get to your question which they probably won't answer because they are too busy reading from their script while they ignore your questions. Don't waste your time, your money or your very sanity. Take a hard pass on this.

Update 6/10/20:
Received an email from Alex with Amazon Executive Support. Apparently the information that we received regarding our 2g/5g internet was not valid. However using an extension cord a long one we positioned the sync module closer to our wifi modem and were finally able to set up the camera. And did get it online. However, that was all.

First of all the 2 year battery life that the description touts is just plain misleading. Apparently this camera will provide that type of battery life if you only arm the camera when you are not at home and have the settings on the lowest functionality, e.g. lowest video quality, lowest sensitivity, shortest video length etc.

Even on the highest settings we the camera just does not "CONSISTENTLY" capture video of motion or people period. Comparing this camera to our blink door bell we are getting about 10% or less video capture of motion/people. However, it does capture video when there is no apparent motion and/people in the activity zones. Also some videos are for 3 seconds or less for who knows what reason.

Not sure why Blink would think that anyone would be happy with this camera and not sure what type of situation this camera would work in since it does not do what it says it does.

This camera is a mystery and is not user friendly. Support is a joke. We have spent so much time trying to figure this camera out it is ridiculous. The Ring camera door bell is much much much easier and 100 times more reliable. We are definitely sending this back.
text_fidelity_b: Blink XT2 Outdoor/Indoor Smart Security Camera with cloud storage included, 2-way audio, 2-year battery life – 2 camera kit

text_fidelity_a:
Razer Kraken BT Kitty Edition: Bluetooth 5.0-40ms Low Latency Connection - Custom-Tuned 40mm Drivers - Beamforming Microphone - Powered Chroma - Quartz Pink The Razer Kraken BT Kitty headset is not a serious gaming headset. The lighting effects and cat ears look cool, and it’s Bluetooth so no wires like the original Kraken Kitty -- those are the big pros.

Razer Synapse does not recognize the headset, so if you want to customize it, two different phone apps are needed.

The Razer Chroma RGB app handles lighting options. The Razer Audio app handles sound settings, firmware updates, and changing the auto shutoff timer.

Do I really want to use my phone to manage my gaming headset? No. I consider having to use my phone while I’m playing a game on my computer to be a hassle!

I did find that I could customize the lighting effects with my phone, unpair the headphones from my phone and then pair them with my computer to keep the lighting effects while using with my computer. But that is also a hassle, considering Razer has a program meant to handle this!

Sound quality is just okay -- it’s not great. I’m not an audiophile so it works for me, but I have less expensive headphones that have better playback, even to my inexperienced ears. The headphones do not have ANC and I miss that a lot.

The controls are basic, a volume wheel and a power button. The power button can be used to pause and play, just hold it in for two seconds and let go, and the music will pause. Hold in for two seconds and let go to resume.

The headphones don’t have a 3.5mm audio jack, they are only Bluetooth. The charging cable is micro USB.

I have the Kraken Kitty wired headset, and I wanted a wireless version because once I started using Bluetooth headphones, I couldn’t stand being chained at my desk by a wire. But I feel like Razer wanted to appeal to women gamers -- make it pink, slap on kitty ears -- and didn’t focus as much on quality or function.
text_fidelity_b: Razer Kraken BT Kitty Edition: Bluetooth 5.0-40ms Low Latency Connection - Custom-Tuned 40mm Drivers - Beamforming Microphone - Powered Chroma - Quartz Pink

Logitech Squeezebox Boom All-in-One Network Music Player / Wi-Fi Internet Radio (Discontinued by Manufacturer) The Squeezebox is a radio that you can use to play internet radio, radio services such as Sirius, and music from your hard drive from anywhere in the house.

Setup is quick and easy. You simply install the Squeezebox software and then create a Squeezebox account. The squeezebox account takes seconds to setup. Once you set it up you tell it what radio services you have. I have a Pandora and Sirius Internet Radio account. You enter your login info, and after it verifies it you are setup.

If you do not have any of these, the wizzard will set one up for you. It also works with services such as Rhapsody and Live365.

Using the Squeezebox software you then identify where you music files are located and where your playlist information is located and then that is done.

You then turn on your radio. It automatically connects to your WIFI connection in your home. Using either the control knob on the box or the remote control you can choose your radio services. Within 10 minutes of UPS delivering the box I was listening to Sirius, Pandora, and my iTunes music from my upstairs bedroom.

The sound is great. Truly exceptional with full deep bass and clear crisp tenor and high ranges. Even at low volumes the unit sounds great.

The unit also has a sleep timer, clock, and alarm features. There are several presets to set so you can choose favorite songs or stations quickly and easily.

Pros: Easy setup, works with mac or pc. Uses existing services you probably already have. Wonderful sound, small design.

Cons: The only real con I see is that the unit is a little pricy. Also the menus on the unit take a little getting used to as there are many menus and options nested within each other.

Overall this is truly a wonderful product. Great sound, easy setup, and ease of use. Truly great for audiophiles.

text_fidelity_a:
Coby Kyros 7-Inch Android 2.3 4 GB Internet Touchscreen Tablet - MID7012-4G (Black) I never owned a tablet or a smartphone so I suppose if I did my review might be different but I think this is a pretty neat little tablet and the price is pretty great too.

I've had it for a couple of days and downloaded the Amazon App store which has most of the apps anyone could need. I mean seriously how many apps does an average person really use? I have downloaded quite a few games for both myself and my kids, the Kindle app, I heart Radio app, and the US newspaper app. So far its holding all of it but I also ordered a microsdhc card for extra space to hold more apps and e-books. I have a regular Kindle that I've had for quite a few years and I am able to transfer most of the books onto this tablet also (I haven't tried downloading all of them since my son uses a few for school). It has where you can calibrate the stylus. Also if you longpress the stylus onto the wallpaper it will let you change the wallpaper in the background.

It does not come with a camera and flashplayer is not installed (but what I understand you can install a "lite" version of flashplayer which I have not done as of yet). The touchscreen is more geared toward using the stylus (which is included) which is a let down to some people. You can use your fingertip but it isn't as responsive as with the stylus IMO. It also comes with a sleeve (that has a place for your stylus) and earphones. There is a charger and a USB cable. There is another cable which I'm not sure exactly what its for (sorry). I haven't used the other cables just yet (except the charger of course). As for battery life it does seem like it runs down pretty quickly (perhaps 3-4 hours). Of course, that may change depending on the type of apps you have running. I know a lot of people worry about reading books from this rather than the Kindle type e-ink. I, personally, like reading at night before I go to sleep and with the Kindle I had to keep a lamp on just to see the page..(barely)...whereas this isn't like that (my eyes are much happier!) You can change the brightness of the screen if you are worried about the brightness bothering your eyes.

I have my email accessible to the Coby Kyros so I can check it throughout the day since my daughter takes off with my laptop quite often. I also downloaded the Dolphin mini browser which I like better than the browser sent with the Kyros. It comes with the GetJar app store which has quite a few apps but Amazon has more.

Of course, I cannot guarantee how well it will hold up because I've only had it for a couple of days but overall its a nice simple little tablet. I've seen the reviews of more expensive tablets and I don't want to spend $400 on a tablet that's rated two stars. I was willing to take the chance and so far I'm happy with my purchase. I rated it 4 stars because the speaker is kinda crappy...I haven't tried listening to the radio with earphones...hopefully it sounds better. And also I wish that it was easier to install flash (I've been looking on the internet but it seems like you have to be really a techie to do it...and I'm not!) It's not an Ipad (or Ipod) so you can't rate this tablet against a product like that (of course it's half the price of a Ipod touch).
text_fidelity_b: Coby Kyros 7-Inch Android 2.3 4 GB Internet Touchscreen Tablet - MID7012-4G (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech HD Webcam C525, Portable HD 720p Video Calling with Autofocus - Black [[VIDEOID:132a9e1a9608d7ddcfd6e870320f72aa]] The 75 second video is intended as a supplement to the written review so that you can see for yourself how well my fairly standard computer can record 720p, and thus get an idea if your computer can benefit from a 720p recording device. This is important to consider because even the manufacturer mentions that many computers cannot keep up with the recording. I mention my system specs in the video.

It's a well designed webcam. It is very small, and the ability to protect its own lens is great. They supply ~5 ft. cord that - wrapped up - takes up about as much room as the camera itself, which allows a connection between a desktop and a separate monitor. Better would have been if they used a standard micro USB connector or some kind of cord wrap system to keep all that out of your way and allow you to use a 30cm cord for connection to your laptop.

The actual optics seem great and the autofocus works pretty well. Even Win XP SP2 allowed me to use the camera function (no video) immediately without installing any software. The software that comes with it eats up nearly 300MB of ROM (that includes their own calling application and editing software that you don't need to install) and only tries caducously to take over your computer (a registry edit and startup menu delete gets rid of unwanted reminders and useless junk running in the background). Oh...I noticed one typo in their software, which is unacceptable, and it also keeps telling me that it doesn't recognize the mic (which is built into the camera), but it records sound anyway.

The design allows for mounting on a monitor 26mm thick or less, but I suppose you could sort of lay it on top of a CRT monitor with no problems. It also allows for a fairly stable mounting on a laptop.

Great device that I would recommend, but I had to take off a star for less than perfect portability and some software blips.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech HD Webcam C525, Portable HD 720p Video Calling with Autofocus - Black

Only issue is the coil whine, which is a roll of the dice. Worst case scenario it'll whine all the time like the first one I tried, whereas my newest replacement only does it during memory tests - which is acceptable.

But other than that, it's excellent. The Carbon and Strix-E both had issues getting my 7200 kit stable at XMP, and I spent almost a week straight tweaking voltages on the Strix - it would always eventually error out in Karhu after 30-60 minutes or so. The Master however is rock solid, and I was able to OC to 7400cl34 with extreme stability. Its "Low Latency/High Bandwidth" options are excellent, and perform better than the XMP tweaked setting on the ASUS.

It also ran the 13900k the coolest, and seemed easier to get stable. Overall if you are lucky enough to not have one with coil whine, it's definitely the best option in this price range.

Great player, otherwise, but if you buy it, assume it will be thrown away and replaced every year or so.

text_fidelity_a:
Creative Zen Sleek Photo 20 GB Multimedia Player (Aluminum/White) I was in the market for a hard drive-based music player and didn't want to go the normal iPxx route, so I began checking into different brands. I had a list of criteria that the player had to meet:

-EXCELLENT SOUND. This is critical. A SnR (Signal to Noise Ratio) of 95db or better

-Excellent battery life. At least 15 hours

-At least 20 GB

-A color screen

-Sturdy build

-As little touch-sensitive controlling as possible. Click wheels are inaccurate and bothersome.

-Ease of use. Drag and drop is preferred.

-AC adapter for charging on the road or from an AC converter in a car

This player meets all of those needs. The SnR is 97db, I've gotten 18 hours out of the battery (remember that increased settings like equalizers and higher bitrates mean lower battery life for ALL players), the case is solid and brushed aluminum, the screen is pretty and quite sharp, only one touch-sensitive control is present, the player CAN drag and drop through Win XP, and it comes with a wall adapter.

I love the powerful sound this puts out and it can drive my big headphones with no problem. It can, like most HDD players, set aside a partition for storage. It has a good FM tuner, recording of FM and a little mic for voice notes. It can even sync with Outlook for contacts and other info. The hard disk seems fast and

Now for the drawbacks:

-You can't watch 15fps video on a tiny screen and reduce your battery life by 67%

-The USB cable is proprietary...no mini USB!

-The wall charger cable plugs into the USB cable...this means two cables for recharging from the wall

-Looking at photos and playing music at the same time is not possible

-Creative software is always iffy. Thankfully, in Win XP, you can open the player from My Computer and access its contents directly with non-DRM music and photos.

-Battery is NON-USER REPLACEABLE. This is odd for Creative.

-No mention of this on the Creative website. Thankfully, updated drivers ARE available from support.

This player would have been state-of-the-art about a year ago, but has been eclipsed by its bigger brother the Zen Vision with 30 and 60GB drives and video...however, if you're not buying into the "kill your eyes with tiny video on tiny screens" and just want a SOLID and RELIABLE player with booming sound, this is it!!! You can tell it's custom-made for Windows (it's MTP, not UMS for any computer), but if you're running XP, then it's a solid choice because you can skip the Creative software and just load music on it.

If you can get it on sale like I did, snatch it up. This is a little gem of a player!
text_fidelity_b: Creative Zen Sleek Photo 20 GB Multimedia Player (Aluminum/White)

Echo Show - 1st Generation Black If there were a way to give this negative stars I'd do it. Amazon, seriously. I don't understand you guys. Half the time you do great things and the other half the time I frankly at am a loss for words. Do you do ANY testing at all before you go to market? Seriously, who decided this was ready to be sold as is.

Me: Alexa show my videos
Echo: Here are your photos.

Me: Alexa show me my movies.
Echo: here are your videos. ( I asked for videos and got photos. I have for movies and it gives me my videos. )
but then it only shows me about 20 of my more than 100 movie Library.

Me: Alexa, show me a calendar
Echo: here is what's on the calendar. (no, I want to see a calendar month for this month)
I tried everything. There is no calendar. If I wanted to see events, I'd ask to see events. See how that is logical? I want to see a calendar. It's not rocket science. It's that basic thing that hangs on everyone's wall? You know a 30 day calendar?

So I begin to think maybe this isn't my account...

Me: Alexa, who's account is this.
Echo: This device has only one account, Alex's.
A last name would be good here. Lot's of Alex's out there.

Me: Alex's show me what's on prime video
Echo: YouTube plays something I have no idea what it is.

I can't ask what's on prime video. It has no concept of what I am asking. And this just goes on and on. Stick with me Amazon. I have an idea. You have a video based Echo. Maybe, just maybe, it would be a good idea that we could ask this video based echo what new movies are on prime video?? Yah think? I eventually got it to show me some prime movies. It seems to pick 20 to show as a selection. Kind of like when it showed me a selection of 20 of my movie library even though I have well over a hundred.

Me: Alexa, show songs from my library.
Echo: this shows 50 random songs from my library.

Me: Alexa, show albums in my library.
Echo: this shows 50 albums. Better than the response I got from my movies query.

Here are some request to make this living disaster better.

Me: Alexa, show me my video collection.
This should result in showing me movies and tv shows I own and/or have rented. I should be able to choose movies from here.
once in movies, I should be able to search for a movie by name from this point.

Me: Alexa, show me a calendar.
This should result in showing me a calendar for the current month, with Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun across the top and all the numbers of the weeks below. I ought to be able to then say, what's going on for the 14th. And it should be the 14th. I should be able to say, add event for the 14th and then add the event. I know, rocket science, right?

Me: Alexa, show me holidays for this month.
The result, I think you know...

If I ask to see my shopping list it says I have one item "1 Song" if I ask it to show me 1 or song or both it fails to understand what I am talking about.

Bottom line, this is JUST NOT FINISHED. Not by a country mile. You have to be kidding me if you think this is ready for the end user.

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech Illuminated Ultrathin Keyboard K740 with Laser-Etched Backlit Keyboard and Soft-Touch Palm Rest - Black This is a very attractive and comfortable keyboard. The keys are fairly responsive (I'd rate them a 7/10 on responsiveness) and have a feel halfway between laptop and regular keyboard. Their noise is diminished when compared to most gaming keyboards but there is still a distinctive soft sound (it's actually quieter than the sound your fingers make if you just lightly drum/tap them on a keyboard without actually typing. Except for the space bar and enter key which are a little louder).

Aesthetics-wise, it is very attractive, the clear plastic edge gives it a nice finished look (though it's of course functionless and breakable, it would protect the keyboard itself and is a seperate molded and attached piece. The lighting is customizable to four settings - off (num lock and caps lock remain on at full brightness at any setting), and then backlights on- low, mid, and high. In general I prefer low lighting and have sensitive eyes and get migraines, and the low setting is pleasant, the higher settings are fine unless you're in the pitch dark and then It's too bright for me. In bright light the top setting is still nice and visible.

The keyboard has all the functions and options like print screen and page up and down and mute/volume controls that I need. I haven't used all of them yet.

The palm/wrist rest is not padded but is comfortable and does have a "soft" feeling coating. It does has sturdy fold out upper feet.

The cord is approximately 71 inches (180 cm).

This is a very slim and comfortable low-profile keyboard that is full size and has great back-lighting options. If it came in multicolor backlighting for a similar price I would've purchased that one as well.

I bought this for a new Lenovo Y910 AIO Win 10 which hasn't arrived yet (thanks UPS for making me wait 3 MORE days now when I paid for 2 day prime shipping), but I tested it on my MSI GE70 laptop running WIn 7 Pro and it was literally plug and play, worked instantly.

The bottom row of keys (ctrl, windows, alt, spacebar, fn, ctrl, are much taller/raised which is a little weird at first (arrow keys and number pad keys match the rest of the low profile keyboard). I may just be noticing it because I have damaged extensor tendons in my dominant left hand which limits how high I can lift 3 of my fingers. Time will tell if I get used to it and stop noticing it.

I've uploaded many photos, one is a composite showing all lighting settings. The differences are much more apparent in person than I could capture on camera.

text_fidelity_a: (2011 Version) Instant Immersion French Levels 1, 2 & 3 I'm terrible at learning languages. I studied French in junior high, high school and a few years in college, but I still had trouble speaking French fluently. I went to Paris a few times and even dated a French native who criticized every word I attempted, so I gave up. Despite this history of failure, I was curious to see if this Instant Immersion French kit would work for me. The box claims that it is just as good, if not better than Rosetta Stone because they refuse to spend as much on advertising. Hmm. I have a hard time believing that advertising is a main reason why Rosetta Stone is popular. The set comes with 4 CDs and the instructions recommend starting with the Ipod audio CD, though the same sheet of instructions say that it should be used as a supplement to the software. As I sampled each disc, I found that the set is really designed less for a serious French student than for a traveler or someone visiting France on business. There is no attempt to teach grammar or language structure, like present or past tense. The lessons all stress memorization and the ability to recognize and parrot standard phrases, remember a good amount of vocabulary (though not the context to use it). I was disappointed to find that it is structured more like a Berlitz language course. Using flashcards and games to learn language is nothing new, and the Oscar Lake game included is absolutely ancient, as I remember this game from 1998. The only "new" thing about this immersion program is the fact it offers an Ipod and interactive DVD option. The interactive DVD was fun to use though the video is low-tech. Also, the quizzes didn't work that well - I had to click my DVD remote arrow buttons several times before it registered my choice. Did all this it work for me? Did my ability to pronounce words improve? So-so. While I enjoyed playing the games and had fun refreshing my memory using the interactive DVD, the kit offers no real revolutionary way to learn language. It all depends on the student and how motivated you are. In that case, I'd probably do well with Berlitz if I'd only tried harder.
text_fidelity_b: (2011 Version) Instant Immersion French Levels 1, 2 & 3
